SCHOOL ROOM · THE ART ROOM · 27 CARDS · AGES 2–5

The Art Room — every card carries a thing to make.

Twenty-seven supplies, twenty-seven activities: draw a picture with shapes, shape a tiny animal, mix two colours together, cut out simple shapes. Every card prints one make-it activity under its name, every supply has its lesson and printable twin right here — and the room runs on the youngest rule in the school: make something, make a mess, make it again.

Open the supply shelf ↓The printable set ↗
HOW THIS ROOM WORKS

Read the card. Make the thing. Then go deeper.

Every card in this deck does two jobs: it names one art supply and it prints one activity — a make-it line the card means literally. The short pages on this shelf show each card, quote its activity word for word, and add one way to set the supply up tonight. When one supply becomes a favorite, its lesson page carries the full teaching — what the tool is, what the activity secretly trains, the parent script, the questions to ask — and the library page holds the printable twin with a download button.

The shelf runs in file order like a real room: the drawing tools first, then the paint and print crew, then the cut-and-stick builders, and the studio furniture at the end. For color work beyond this room, the Colors extra class hunts every shade the house hides, and the Coloring Pages keep print-and-color days stocked when the paints are still drying from yesterday.

ALL TWENTY-SEVEN SUPPLIES

Meet the shelf — cover to watercolors.

Every card in the owner’s file order: chalk, clay, colored pencils and cotton balls open the shelf; crayons, paint, scissors and glue carry the middle; and the studio furniture closes it. Read every card right here on this page.

GAMES THE ART ROOM PLAYS

When the glue is drying, play.

Art time and game time trade places all afternoon, and the school’s games shelf holds the rules for the games this room plays best: the Colour Hunt turns the whole house into a color deck, the Shape Hunt finds the shapes chalk pictures are built from, Shadow Shapes poses drawings against the wall, and Follow the Leader is a copy-me drawing game with no pencil at all. Full rules on every page — the paint pots can wait.

AROUND THE SCHOOL

Where to wander next.

Explore the School — every room, one door each ↗Print a Coloring Page for quiet table time ↗Hunt colors in the Colors extra class · Ages 2–5 ↗

The Art Room sits on the school’s room shelf beside the Library, the Garden, the Playground and the Music Room. The Colors class is its closest cousin — fifteen spotter sheets for the shades this room paints with — and the Coloring Pages are its quiet corner: bold outlines, one download each, no setup at all.

Making is the curriculum. Every activity on these cards hides real work — grips, pressure, planning, patience — inside something the child thinks is just today’s craft. Do the thing first; the skills follow the glue.

HOLIDAY CRAFTS

Make it for the celebration.

Every holiday needs glue: paper ghosts and painted pumpkins for Halloween, handprint turkeys for Thanksgiving, hearts for Valentine’s Day, crescent moons for Eid. The school’s School Hall keeps the holiday calendar — the next celebration first — and every holiday page there carries printable cards that pair with the make-it activities in this room: craft here, celebrate there.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 27 cards in Art Room, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Art Room. We have 27 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Chalk

    “Chalk! Let’s draw with shapes — a big circle for the sun, a square for the house, a triangle on top for the roof. What other shapes can our picture hold?”

    How: Draw one giant shape on the ground — circle, square or triangle — and let the child fill it with more shapes until the whole thing is a shape mosaic. Rain will wash the gallery clean, which is half the fun.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Clay

    “Clay! Roll it, roll it, roll it — now we have a little body. Pinch two ears, press a nose — what animal is growing in your hands?”

    How: Start with one ball and let the child decide what it becomes. Keep a damp cloth nearby so the clay stays soft, and give the finished animal a name — named animals get siblings, and siblings mean the next round is already booked.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Colored Pencils

    “Colored pencils! Hold the pencil low and lay it down flat — sweep, sweep, sweep like the wind. Look, the apple is turning red from one side to the other!”

    How: Draw one big outline — an apple, a ball, a leaf — and shade only one side of it, dark to light. The object suddenly looks round, and the child has just invented 3-D without being told.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Cotton Balls

    “Cotton balls! Dip, dip, dab — bounce the soft cloud across the paper. Puff, puff — our sky is filling up with paint clouds!”

    How: Clip a clothespin around a cotton ball to give the cloud a handle, then dab a whole sky. Blue paint for day, purple for storm, and one flat smear for the rainbow that always follows.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Craft Sticks

    “Craft sticks! Two sticks here, two sticks there — a little square house for our picture. Where should the frame hang?”

    How: Glue four sticks into a square and let the child decorate the frame before the picture goes in — frames deserve art too. A strip of tape behind the corners holds everything while the glue dries overnight.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Crayon

    “Crayon! Pick your colors — red, orange, yellow, green! Draw the sun, draw a flower, draw a big wobbly something. A picture with ten colors is a RAINBOW picture!”

    How: Tape three crayons together and draw with a triple line at once — then split them apart and see which marks each color made alone. The child has just met the idea that tools change the drawing.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Drawing Pad

    “Drawing pad! Open the book to a new page — now draw your favorite thing in the whole world. A dog? A truck? Pancakes? Fill the page with it!”

    How: Turn a page into a gallery: child draws the favorite thing in the middle, then you draw yours beside it, then trade pages and add one detail to each other’s picture. Two artists, one book, zero wrong answers.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Easel

    “Easel! Clip the paper on tight, choose your paint, and stand like a real painter. Lean back a little — look at your work! Artists always step back to see the whole picture.”

    How: Set the easel by a window and paint what the child actually sees outside — the same tree, painted four times a year, becomes a diary that draws itself. No easel? Prop a clipboard on a chair back and the studio travels.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Eraser

    “Eraser! Rub, rub, rub — the shape is gone! Now draw it again, even better this time. See? Paper gives us second tries. That is the secret power of the eraser.”

    How: Draw a circle, erase half of it, and redraw the missing part as a moon, a cookie with a bite, a letter C. One shape, three ideas — the eraser is the doorway between them.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Feathers

    “Feathers! Feel how soft — now a dot of glue, press it down, one, two, three. Our picture has real feathers! A bird that never flies off the page!”

    How: Draw a big bird body, then glue real feathers along the wing line, one row at a time. Count them as they land — the bird that ends up with fourteen feathers is the fanciest bird in the house.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Glue

    “Glue! A little dot, a little dot — not too much! Press the paper down and count to ten. One, two, three... ten! Stuck forever. What comes next on our collage?”

    How: Tear old magazine pages into strips and build a collage of one big shape — a tree, a whale, a letter of the child’s name. Dots of glue, not rivers: the child learns the difference the first time a river wrinkles the paper.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Ink

    “Ink! One little press with one little finger — look! The tiniest lines inside your finger made a pattern nobody else has. Press again — same pattern, new print!”

    How: Press a row of fingerprints and add legs, wings or hats with a pen — a caterpillar of thumbs, a flock of pinky birds. Every print carries the child’s own swirls, which makes it the most personal stamp in the world.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · Markers

    “Markers! Cap off — CHEK! Now draw a bold line... all the way across! Loud lines, quiet lines, wiggly lines. What sound does a zigzag make?”

    How: Play a line orchestra: one long steady line (a hum), three short sharp lines (a drumbeat), a slow wavy line (a song). The paper becomes sheet music, and the marker plays it.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Paintbrush

    “Paintbrush! Dip in the paint — swoosh across the paper, all the way to the edges! We are painting the SKY first. The background comes first, and then the picture lands on top.”

    How: Paint the whole page one bright color and let it dry, then draw on top with crayon — crayon on paint is a picture with a sunset inside it. Big brush for backgrounds, small brush for details: that is the studio rule.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Palette

    “Palette! Here is red, here is yellow — swirl them round and round... ORANGE! You made a brand-new color! What happens if red meets blue instead?”

    How: Mix one drop of white into each color on the palette and line the originals next to their paler twins — a wall of light versions. Then try the dark side with one drop of black, and let the child name the inventions.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Paper Plate

    “Paper plate! Turn it over — look, it is already a face shape! Where do the eyes go? High up! Where is the nose? In the middle! Now the silliest smile ever!”

    How: Build the face in layers: draw it, then glue on button eyes, yarn hair and a paper-tube nose. Hold it up to your own face and let the plate talk — funny voices are what turn craft time into theater.

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Paper

    “Paper! Fold it this way... and this way... open the ears — look, a puppy! What should our paper animal be called? Every fold changed the paper into something new!”

    How: Fold a square in half corner to corner for a triangle — that triangle is a cat with two fold-up ears, and it stands on its own. Add whiskers with a pencil and the whole animal took one minute.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Pencil

    “Pencil! Draw a big oval — an egg shape! Two eyes, a little nose, and a mouth. Is it smiling? Is it surprised? You just drew a PERSON!”

    How: Draw the same face three times with three mouths — happy, surprised, grumpy — and watch one sketch become three feelings. Add a mirror: the child draws their own face, which is the hardest and funniest portrait of all.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Ribbon

    “Ribbon! Look how it bends — swoop! Make a big loop, now a squiggle, now a zigzag. A dot of glue... and the ribbon stays exactly where we put it. Our picture has REAL lines!”

    How: Glue ribbon lines onto paper and turn them into a picture: one ribbon becomes a road for a drawn car, another becomes the tail of a drawn kite. Then hold the leftover ribbon high and run — because ribbon play is air play.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Ruler

    “Ruler! Press it down flat — one hand holds, one hand draws. Whoosh — a perfectly straight line! Two more... three! Nobody’s line is straighter than ours today.”

    How: Draw three straight lines and let the child tell you what they become: a table needs four, a road needs two, a ladder needs a dozen. Then flip the ruler over and connect the tick marks — the numbers are already a counting game.

  24. Cards 21–27
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Scissors

    “Scissors! Thumb on top — open... close... snip! Look, a circle is being born! Slow snips make the shape smooth. What shape comes next?”

    How: Draw a fat triangle, a square and a wavy snake line, then cut all three. The snake is the graduation exam: wavy lines are where scissor hands become steady. Snippets do not get wasted — they become the confetti pile for tomorrow’s glue.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Sponge

    “Sponge! Dip in the paint — press down... lift! Look, a print! Again — press, lift, press, lift! Same shape again and again: that is called a PATTERN.”

    How: Cut a dry sponge into small shapes with cookie-cutter edges — a square, a heart, a star — and print rows of each. Every press lands slightly crooked, and the crookedness is what makes sponge prints look handmade, because they are.

  27. 24
    Card 23 · Stamps

    “Stamps! Press in the ink — tap, tap. Now press on the paper — push down hard and... LIFT! A perfect star! Again! A whole ROW of stars, all the same!”

    How: Print a border around a page’s edge — one shape, one row per side — and the next letter written inside it becomes a decorated letter. Then mix two stamps and let the child invent the repeating rule: star, flower, star, flower.

  28. 25
    Card 24 · Stencil

    “Stencil! Hold it down tight with one hand — the shape is hiding inside. Trace around the edge... lift it up — a perfect star! Your hand did that!”

    How: Trace the same stencil twice, sliding it a little the second time, and color the space between the two outlines — the shape grows a rainbow echo. Letters work the same way: stencil the child’s initial, then fill it with marker dots.

  29. 26
    Card 25 · Stickers

    “Stickers! Peel it — see the shiny back? Press it on the paper... stuck! Another one, and another — look, our stickers are making a picture! What is it becoming?”

    How: Draw a big scene lightly in pencil — a garden, a road, the night sky — and let the stickers move in as the stars, the cars, the flowers. Peeling the backing is the finger gym; placing them without overlap is the puzzle.

  30. 27
    Card 26 · Tape

    “Tape! Rip off a piece — rrrrip! Press it across both papers — pat, pat, pat. Look! Two papers are holding hands now! What can tape join next?”

    How: Tape paper strips into links and build a paper chain — every link is one rip, and the chain grows longer than the child, which is the goal every time. Colored tape on plain paper also makes roads, rails and racing tracks for toy cars.

  31. 28
    Card 27 · Watercolors

    “Watercolors! Brush in the water first, then the paint — sweep it across, soft and slow. A little more water... even softer! Our sky is turning into a real one.”

    How: Paint the sky wet-on-wet: brush clean water over the paper first, then touch color into the wet and watch it bloom by itself. Drop one extra dot in the middle and call it the sun coming out — the water does the painting.

  32. 29
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  33. 30
    Check

    “Can you find Chalk? Now show me Paintbrush.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  34. 31
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 27 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
